utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are a couple of preliminaries --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your microphone is not activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies. A couple of preliminaries to save time. First, just dealing with the two potential exhibits that the witness produced. The leaflet I'm unable either to accept or reject or challenge that that's a genuine document dropped by NATO. I have no position on that one way or the other. Second, the transcript of the alleged communication between the pilot and base is something that's dealt with in Exhibit D323, which was the report to the Prosecutor on the NATO bombing that the accused put in, and it can be found there at paragraph 66, which I'll just lay on the overhead projector, if Mr. Nort would be so good, and this will explain my position on that. It is claimed, it says, by one source, report on file with OTP. The other passage, please, Mr. Nort. Further up. No, further up. The paragraph 66. Can you push the page up, please. "It is claimed --" Mr. Nort, that's it. "It is claimed by one source (report on file with the OTP) that the Yugoslav TV broadcast of the attack on the Djakovica convoy on the 15th of April recorded a conversation between one F-16 pilot involved in the attack and the AWACS. This conversation is alleged to establish both that the attack on the convoy was deliberate and that a UK Harrier pilot had advised the F-16 pilot that the convoy was comprised solely of tractors and civilians. The F-16 pilot was then allegedly told that the convoy was nevertheless a legitimate military target and was instructed to fire on it. This same report also suggests that the convoy was attacked with cluster bombs, indicated by bomb remnants and craters left at the site. However, these claims - both with regard to the foreknowledge of the pilot as to the civilian nature of the convoy and of the weapons used - are not confirmed by any other source." I haven't yet been able to track down the report on file with the OTP to identify the single source that is referred to there, but it is sufficient to observe both that there appears to have been one source, it may be this book, making this claim, and at the time of the preparation of this report that no other sources had been identified. That remains our position, and if it changes, I'll let the Court know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the evidence has now identified a number of sources. The witness has told us that this was widely broadcast on television, and it may be that the matter is worth further inquiry now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've started the process of inquiries, but so far we haven't been able to confirm that it's been broadcast in any other source. Third point that I mention, I'm not going to ask questions about it in light of the absolutely emphatic position of this witness that Bela Crkva was no -- no action and no KLA. He can't have been clearer on that. The Chamber may possibly recall, and if it hasn't been told this already I should just draw it to your attention, the book of the fallen heroes of the KLA contains some ten names that match names of those killed in Bela Crkva. There are seven Popajs, and three Zuniqis. There is no explanation for why they're in the book and the Chamber will recall that various possibilities have been advanced as to why names may be in that book other than people being in any sense active members of the KLA or supporters of it, but nevertheless I simply draw that to your attention so that the point won't be missed but I'm not going to ask the witness anything about it. The final point, which brings me to my resumption of cross-examination is this: The witness, yesterday, in using the word "ciscenje" started to give an explanation that used the word "separate," and I intervened at that stage to suggest that on no occasion had he used the phrase "separate" before when I'd given him a careful opportunity to consider the position. His Honour Judge Robinson observed that the witness had used that definition earlier in the day. I have to say I thought that His Honour may have been in error, but we've checked the transcript, and the position appears to be that the only use of the word "separation" as an explanation of or definition of the word "ciscenje" was given by Djosan in his interposed cross-examination. What happened was, and I'd like the witness to follow this because I want to ask him two more questions about it, that in the absence of the witness - and it was on day 433 but I don't have the time for it, I'm afraid; it's page 45950 - he was asked by me, in respect of the way it had been translated: "'Ciscenje' means -- it's been translated as 'mopping up,' but does it also mean 'cleansing'?" Djosan said: "No. 'Ciscenje' means separating the good from the bad." "If you take it --" I asked: "Does it?" And he answered: "If you take it as a word. That meant separating the terrorists from the rest of the population." My recollection, confirmed by a search of LiveNote, is that there was no further use of the word "separation" as synonymous with or defining of the word in which we have an interest until at 12.24 and 59 seconds yesterday this witness gave the answer that he did. And unless I'm shown to be in error on that, unless I'm -- there's a part of the transcript that has this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thought I heard it yesterday earlier in the evidence. Djosan didn't give evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, he didn't, but we've checked the transcript against the word "separation" or "separate," and it simply doesn't appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And with that preamble, Mr. Vukovic, when you used the words yesterday as follows, you said this: "This refers to 'ciscenje,' the cleaning or cleansing exclusively as part of an operation against terrorists, just as you use the word 'cleaning' in everyday life where you separate --" and then there was a reference to "good from bad." I want to know why you suddenly decided to use that definition, separate, for this particular word.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I suddenly decided to use that phrase. I was trying but you didn't allow me. You interrupted me mid-sentence. I was just trying to explain what is meant when that notion is used in military terminology. In your long introduction, you said something that was wrong. I never stated that there had been no action in Bela Crkva. How can I say anything? Maybe there was some action there yesterday. I stated that there wasn't any action on the 25th of October in Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... which is about the use of the word "ciscenje" and its definition by separation. My suggestion to you is very simple: That between the very first day of your evidence when you gave -- the first day of your cross-examination by me when I was only able to ask you questions for about ten minutes, I must suggest to you you've been in discussion with someone, either with Djosan himself or with someone else who has explained to you how you're going to get round the problem of this use of the word "ciscenje." Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't have a problem at all. It seems that you have a problem. You know full well, as I do, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel. Colonel. Colonel, just answer the question. The suggestion is that you have been in discussion with somebody who advised you how to get around the problem of the word "ciscenje" by giving it the meaning separating good from bad. Have you been in discussion with anybody? Were you in discussion with anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not in discussion with anybody in relation to this trial because that is forbidden for witnesses while they give testimony. Even later, they're not allowed to talk to potential witnesses, and I fully abide by that. I would not bring myself and my family into a situation that would lead to you punishing me by a measure which is fully justified if such a thing happened. So I never discussed any such thing like what Mr. Nice just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, did you see the evidence of Djosan or did you read a review of it in any newspaper to allow yourself to be affected by what he'd said?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I was not in a position to see the general's testimony, General Djosan's evidence. On that note, I haven't been buying newspapers since I got here because I have better things to do. I came on a completely different assignment. Even what I do is too strenuous for me, let alone reading newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have definitions from a Croatian or a Serbian/English dictionary. I don't think I can usefully ask questions of the witness about a definition because one goes through the words. I can simply tell you that the word "separate" doesn't appear in any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn to one other matter of detail before I leave Bela Crkva. I suggested to you yesterday that there was no evidence of the buildings of Bela Crkva being damaged after the incidents of the 25th of March. That needs correction. If we can lay on the overhead projector, in order to correct it, "As Seen, As Told" first of all at page 278. Yes. If we look at this, please, on the left-hand side. There is a paragraph that reads as follows, and I'm reading this out for your assistance, Mr. Vukovic. There's a paragraph that says of the Bela Crkva event: "Surviving villagers who had either remained or --"

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me find it, please. I haven't found it. You could --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Bela Crkva entry, two paragraphs before the headline "Celine."

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Surviving villagers who had either remained or failed to escape Bela Crkva, were eventually expelled from the village on or around the 16th of April, when the police entered at approximately 15.00 hours and told everyone to leave in 30 minutes under threat being killed by the VJ. Later the same day, three large, heavily armed groups of soldiers with paint on their faces entered the village. The police forced two young brothers to undress, they fired their guns close to the boys, then released them after forcing them to hand over 1.060 Deutschmarks." And then this: "As everyone was leaving the village, the police burned the houses after looting them, and cars were confiscated." So you follow, Mr. Vukovic, that there is some evidence of some houses, I would suggest the residue, being burnt on the 16th of April, but otherwise the evidence is to the effect that the houses were burnt in the initial attack on the 25th of March. And I'd like to now, just to tidy this issue up, to look at two versions of Exhibit 320, tab 74. This is aerial views of the damage to Bela Crkva, and what we've -- what the Court will see first of all on the screen is the exhibit as it's presently formed, and the disadvantage -- sorry, that's -- no, the other one first, please. No, the other -- can you put the other document on, please, Mr. Nort, so that I can explain it. Not that. That's it. No, not that one. The other one. If you bring it back, I'll show you so that I can explain what we've done. Now, if you put that on, the original exhibit of two aerials dated -- two aerial pictures of the 11th of March and the 2nd of April show the same location but the one on the right is oriented opposite -- in an opposite way from the one on the left. So now please put the other document on the screen, and what we've done is turn the right-hand one around so you can see. That's fine. Now, if you look at this -- it's the original exhibit, we've just tidied up the orientation. If you look at this from the aerial views, this, you see, Mr. Vukovic, shows damage that could be seen from the air of the same locations, not on a later date when the last people from Bela Crkva were cleared out but on the 11th of March, and then the 2nd of April. So there is a large amount of damage that is absolutely visible there. Can you explain, please, how that happened?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in the introduction, which was again very long, you said that it was clear. I think that you are assuming that that's clear. But I'm telling you that on the 25th of March, not a single house in Bela Crkva was destroyed or torched. That's what you've been trying to say all the time, as if I had stated that. On the 16th of April I was not at this locality because it was outside the zone of action of my battalion. I cannot talk about the 16th because I do not have relevant information. Further on, as for these photographs, you've been showing me some photographs, black and white, of dubious provenance, to put it mildly. First of all, I don't understand English so could you please tell me who took those photographs and where from so that I know that that is exactly when they were taken, when you say they were taken. Tell me the source. Who took these photographs? Was it NATO perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, it's not for you to make demands or requests of that kind. These are aerial photographs of the dates given, produced in evidence before this Court. My question to you is a simple one. It will be, of course, for the learned Judges to decide whether to accept these photographs as what they have been produced as, but please tell us, if it is found that these photographs reliably show what was to be seen on the 2nd of April at Bela Crkva and on the 11th of March, can you explain for us - yes or no - how the damage was caused?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot explain it. All of yesterday I've been -- I was explaining that there was no action in Bela Crkva. How can I explain the difference between those two photographs? I'm telling you, I am expressing my suspicion with regard to the provenance of the photographs, and you convince me otherwise. You want me to give an answer to a question related to something that I claim never happened. I cannot assist you on that note or the Trial Chamber, or could I be of assistance to Mr. Milosevic had he put that kind of ambiguous question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to look at another map which picks up the proposition I was putting to you yesterday, and by this I want to conclude dealing with Bela Crkva, and I hope the Court will understand me if I don't -- I hope the Court will understand if I don't deal with other sites in detail, but there isn't time and the generality of my case has been advanced through Bela Crkva and the issues that that raises. Remember yesterday, Mr. Vukovic, we were looking at a map on an easel which was hard to see, despite all the best efforts of the audiovisual unit. I have tried -- or we have attempted to convert material on that map into a different format and it's quite easy to follow. This is a map which is an exhibit in the case, schematic rather than a detailed map, showing the relevant area, and you can confirm that if we look at the red line of the road it goes from the crossing at Cafa Prusit, which is on the left of the map, it goes through the location Zub, from where you were to start your march, it then runs through Djakovica and would run through Prizren and then back to the other potential crossing at Vrbica. Those matters of geography, am I accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Just a minute, Mr. Milosevic has a point to make.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it would be fair to the witness to translate what it says in the heading of the map. In the heading, it says that this is a map that shows the activities from Vukovic's diary of the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade. That is what Mr. Nice showed to the witness, but he did not tell him that this map depicts activities from his diary, and he should know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Activities of cleaning, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish the accused would not interrupt and try and tell me how to run the questioning. I'm coming to matters in the appropriate order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a fair point. Let the witness have the full context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was coming to that in due course, and this is simply a map, and I'm now going to explain the use to which we've made of the map. First of all, the witness has, I think, confirmed that the road is as I've described it, which is the red line. We now come to the entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, you've heard what the accused has read out and so I needn't go into it again, but if you look at the left-hand side of this map -- perhaps audiovisual would make the left-hand side, or Mr. Nort could make the left-hand side -- left-hand side, thank you, available. Starting at the top. Starting at the top. Marvelous. What we have done here, Mr. Vukovic, is take the entries from the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. diary of your unit where they referred to cleaning or cleansing activities, and we've coded them by colour where possible. So that if you look at the map at the top box in red, that shows how on the 25th of March in your diary, war diary, and on our reading of the diary - you can check or otherwise - it marks Bela Crkva, Celine, Nogavac, and Velika Krusa as blocked and cleaned. If we then take the red colour and look on the map itself, we'll see the position of those four villages. The next box down reflects the entry in your diary for the 26th of March, continue cleaning in cooperation with MUP. The villages are right Randubrava, Retimlje, Donje Retimlje and Velika Krusa. They're green in the code on the left; they're green on the map. The third entry, in orange, for the 27th of March, a similar entry dealing with Donje Retimlje, Neprebiste, Zojic, Medregovac, and Mamusa, and we can see the orange marks on the map. The next entry, which is in black, doesn't -- for the 28th of March, doesn't refer to any cleaning or cleansing but refers to 2.000 people going through the crossing, which is the crossing on the westerly part of the map. I'll run through the whole of the map so that you can have the context. Purple is next for the 29th of March, and those villages can be seen at the top. Slightly -- at the top of the map, near where the blue marks are, the blue rectangles are marked. And you will recall that the blue rectangles are the villages or towns that you accepted as being KLA strongholds. And on the same day, the 29th of March, there was reference to 1.000 people crossing the border at Cafa Prusit. On the 30th of March, in yellow, there's reference to cleaning the villages of Rogovo and mahala Postra, and yellow is marked, as we can see, on the map. The 31st of March, in dark blue, refers again to the villages of Ostrozub and Madjare, which is up at the top in the area of the KLA strongholds. And finally, there is a pale green for the 1st of April, dealing with Pagarusa and Milanovic, and those can be seen towards the north of the map, just underneath the KLA strongholds. So that this map reflects what your diary shows; namely, an advance from the west going through the red villages, then the green villages, then the orange villages. Only after that venturing up into the area of the KLA strongholds on the 29th of March, dealing with Rogovo where the special unit, the 72nd unit was involved in cooperation with you on the 30th of March, dealing with the KLA stronghold areas again on the 31st of March, and then with two villages south of that on the 1st of April. Do you accept that that map shows by colour coding the pattern of cleaning operations done by your unit?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that at all. First of all, I don't accept the map at all, Mr. Nice, and we'll be able to see this best on the big map. I have it here but I don't know why you are consistently avoiding that map. You have provided a map here that is quite distorted and which doesn't mean a thing to any soldier. A topographic map is the only thing that a soldier can follow properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, will you please observe some manners and not continually try to make adverse comments about the way I am asking you questions. This map is a map that has been used by this Court for three and a half years and they have found it helpful. It is a schematic map. It shows villages in their position relative one to the other. Will you now please focus on my question and say why the simple propositions I've advanced to you are inaccurate, given that they come from your diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, bear in mind, Mr. Nice, he has said he doesn't find the map helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what he says, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He did say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He said that, Your Honour, but this witness, even more than the others, has occupied the Court's time in an effort to be combative with me in a way that, in my respectful submission, is quite inappropriate and I would ask the Court to ensure that he answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, he's entitled, in my view, to say that he doesn't find the map helpful. You may ask him why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he didn't say that, as far as I can see. He said he didn't accept the map. I don't think he's talking about helpfulness or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He wanted a topographic map, which is the Delic-style maps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can be of assistance if you will allow me. Why don't I think it's helpful? Because there are a lot of mistakes. And in the first instance I saw -- well, anybody who wants to can try and find the village of Medikovac [phoen]. I know where it is in Kosovo and Metohija, and I was personally in that village, and it is quite to the north, far north, at the very administrative border, that is to say between the province of Kosovo and Metohija and Serbia proper. And it is in the Podujevo municipality. So go ahead, then. Find the village of Medakovo on this map. That is why I say that this is a very, very bad copy. I have the original map here, the original map of that terrain dating back to those times, so can we put that map up and see what happened, where, when? Otherwise, these are not valid data from my diary, because as far as I was able to understand the interpretation given of what Mr. Milosevic said, it would appear that with my unit I went right up to Prizren and the Brunic pass, whereas I never was there. I was in Prizren professionally in the brigade command but never with my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give me again the name of the village you're inviting us to locate on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Medregovac, where it says Medregovac. That village is in the Podujevo municipality. 200 metres into the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. I can give you the names and surnames of the people who live there: The Ibovic family - I was there myself - the Bulatovics live there, several -- four or five families living there, and some ten Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because it is an exclusively Serb village, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is that a mistake --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be a mistake of that particular word. It doesn't affect --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be a mistake of that particular word. It doesn't affect the generality, and I'm going to press on because time is limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can I ask the witness: Are there any other villages wrongly identified on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I would need at least half an hour to compare this map with the original topographical map, because, as far as I can see, the names are given in the Siptar -- in the Siptar and Serbian languages. I'd like to look at it in greater detail so that I can give a proper response, and I just happened to glance at this and make that remark, note that, because it says that my unit was there in that village on the 27th of March, and I know that it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I was just going to say, Mr. Nice, if the witness is not prepared to answer on the basis of the map, then no doubt we can look at maps of the area in due course and note the point you're making if he can't assist us on the basis of what is actually being produced to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm obliged and I'm going to take one more opportunity to see if he will confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just look at the map in general terms, Mr. Vukovic. Allow for the possibility that Medregovac is an error perhaps of reading a handwritten document. Am I right in suggesting to you that in general terms your units moved from the area where the red villages are marked on the first day to the green villages on the second day, to the orange villages on the third day? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, that is correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that they were moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, if you would be so good as to look at another document which is extracted from Delic's war diary entries, and you may or may not be able to confirm it. Just have a look at this, please. We've used the same colour coding to see where Delic's troops were according to his diary which is, as the Court knows, late produced and still in the process of translation. I've got some translations done but I've got a feeling it take too long to put documents through this witness, and I'll just see if he'll confirm it. Do you accept that Delic, on the 25th of March -- and we used the same colour coding on the left-hand side from his diary, and we've used the same colour coding in the dots. Do you accept that on the 25th of March his troops were in the area of Retimlje?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But please, would you first read out and translate for me the title of the map, the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The map reflects, since you wish to have the title, the location of actions from entries in Delic's diary of the 52nd Motorised Brigade. Now, will you please answer my question. To your knowledge - it's a very simple question - were Delic's troops in the area of Retimlje on the 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th and 26th and 27th they were part of the 549th Motorised Brigade, or part of it was in Retimlje village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And indeed you picked up the point. He gives in his diary explanation of the troops being in Retimlje, Dobrodeljane and Pagarusa on the 26th, marked in green; in the same three places on the 27th; and in Dobrodeljane, Pagarusa marked in pink on the 28th; and in those same two places on the 29th. So that for the first five days of operation, as your troops were moving west to east, his troops were in a blockade position on the north-south axis running from Pagarusa down to Retimlje. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not accept that. If you take a look at the order of the brigade commander for this anti-terrorist operation - and I'll provide it for you, it is in my binder, tab number 2, unless I'm mistaken -- no, number 3, map number 3 - and if you take a look at his decision, which I have as number 4, you will be able to see that what you're saying is quite incorrect. So the line was taken up, the blockade line was taken up first over a large area. The Orahovac, Suva Reka, Velika Krusa area is quoted, so that means a broader region with three points, and that's how you denote an area. You give three points. And then part of the unit remained in the blockade, or at the blockade, along the road from Zrze towards Prizren so as to prevent the Siptar terrorist forces pulling out towards the Albanian border and linking up with those forces who were active on the other side. Let me remind you that the night between the 25th, 4th and 5th is when the aggression started on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and we expected that there would be action on the ground as well. And the second part was in a blockade, but as I say, this -- it is difficult to discern and interpret this map because I cannot differentiate a stream from a road, for example. Everything has been entered in black. But anyway, it was somewhere behind Suva Reka, in this area here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice will put another question to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The order in advance of the march and the action is only a forecast of what is to come. You accepted to me yesterday that obviously contemporaneous records of what actually happened are likely to be more valuable than anything else. The markings on this map reflect what is actually in Delic's war diary. Do you see? This is where he says his troops were. And I'm just going to finish the point because if you look at the same map, please, or visual aid or whatever we call it, we see that on the 29th of March, and according to his diary, he was in Dobrodeljane-Pagarusa; on the 30th of March, in yellow, he was in Ljubiste, Vranic, Medakovo and Macitevo, which is marked to the top and to the west. And on the 31st of March, according to his diary, in Ljubiste, Vranic, Budakovo and Macitevo that's marked in dark blue. So that the position is as follows, and it may be you don't actually dispute this, that as you were driving in from the west, Delic's forces were available as a blockade on the east, and subsequently his troops provided cover on the west. All of this, I must suggest to you, having the effect of driving the people moved out of these villages onto the main road and from the main road to Albania, and that's what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what -- I have to say that you're not right on that point again. There wasn't a blockade either on the west or on the north. What was blocked was the broader region, a much wider area than the area which we thought the terrorists were in. And we started searching the terrain. I can see you're not listening to me, but never mind. That's my answers aren't clear to you. As I was saying, we started out from a circle -- we searched the terrain in the form of a circle --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course I'm listening to you, Mr. Vukovic. But, Your Honours, I really must request the Chamber to preserve the dignity of the Court by stopping this witness in his attempted insolence. It's been a characteristic of many of the accused's witnesses. I've wondered whether its rehearsed because it has a pattern about it. I'm a very tolerant man, but there are limits, and the Court must, in my respectful submission, stop witnesses doing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber is monitoring the witnesses. Mr. Vukovic, just answer the questions. I've warned you before: Leave aside the comments, just answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be clear: What I was saying is that your assertion is not correct, and if you would like to hear why, I shall give you the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Explain why, please.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to have this map, if possible, placed on the easel so that I can explain this to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be placed on the easel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While that's being done, Mr. Nice, I take it that the heading for this should actually be the 549th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the 549th. It was done overnight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this map you can see everything very well, that what was blocked was the broader area from Orahovac, Velika Krusa, and Suva Reka. I say broader region, which doesn't mean that these places were blocked as well, the places themselves, villages. And here we can see the deployment of my units along the blockade line. Here on the asphalt road, as you can see, there was a unit there, and that unit throughout the whole operation, from the 25th to the 27th, that is, was located along the blockade line. It did not move away from there. And its task was to prevent terrorist forces from passing towards the south and going to the border with Albania. And I think you'll be able to find in the diary what happened, that is that in the region of the village at Pirane on the 26th, if I remember correctly, fewer terrorists or, rather, the -- some of the forces had been routed but other remaining terrorists tried to pull out through the positions of the forces setting up the blockade and they were prevented in doing that. There was another unit that was along the blockade line throughout. It was at this line here from Donja Srbica, but Donja Srbica once again was not blocked itself. You can see these positions quite clearly. All the rest of the units, all the other units of the combat group which had been established for this anti-terrorist operation had the assignment and task by 6.00 on the 25th, take up the -- their positions at the blockade line on a circular basis, in a circle, because only -- you only do that in an anti-terrorist operation. And then to move from all directions, from all axes simultaneously in uncovering and finding and breaking up or destroying or taking prisoner, if you prefer, the terrorists. And you will not be able to find any such assignment whereby action was taken towards the civilian population at all. That was never done. There was no action against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Chamber has heard enough about this matter and whether it was helpful or not, because I want to move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please do. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vukovic. You can sit down. Since you refer to maps, this much is absolutely clear, isn't it: The map that's produced of the plan is an advanced plan, an advanced -- a plan showing -- a map showing an advanced plan of what was supposed to happen. Yes?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a plan with all the forecasts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Commanders with maps sometimes mark their maps with what actually happens.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On these maps, we do not mark what actually happened. This map is compiled before an action starts. So it is a decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying that there's no example that you know of a military commander marking where his troops are and then rubbing it out and putting them where they've gone and -- maps are never used like that in the Yugoslav army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying, but not this particular map. This particular map represents a decision. It is a working map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So were there maps at the time which actually had people like you and the other commanders marking on them what they actually did as opposed to what they were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, you see: As the commander of a combat group, I had a map of this terrain where I personally recorded the positions of my units, introduced the position of my units and the most important axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where is that map, please?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, allow me to finish. It is a working map. Truth to tell, it is kept in the units of the rank of a battalion, but once an analysis has been performed, the map is destroyed by burning, and that is what is stated in instructions and guidelines for the work of staff and headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the map?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what the instructions tell us to do. For example, this is a lasting document, a permanent document, Mr. Nice, that is stored and kept together with the order and an analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm only too happy to see these instructions. Do you have them with you, which say that maps have to be destroyed? It may be the case, I don't know, I'm just interested to see it. Have you got the instruction with you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not "may be," it's certainly that way. I'm a trained, educated officer, and I tell you that that is so, and I will be able to procure a booklet telling you things like that. Working maps kept by larger units are secret, confidential ones, but the company, battalion, or platoon level doesn't. So I'm talking about this on the basis of my own unit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreter didn't understand the witness properly because it says those maps, it says in the transcript secret documents, and the witness said not "tajni" but "trajni," permanent documents. The witness did not say "tajni" but "trajni," which means not secret but permanent, lasting. You can ask him again, if you like. The maps that are lasting documents, permanent documents, because he is -- was explaining what, according to instructions, are permanent, lasting documents and what aren't. Of course, documents that aren't permanent are destroyed. You have shredders yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, you said something about working maps of larger units being kept, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So did you say that they were in some way secret?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... did you say that they were in some way permanent?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that they were of a permanent character.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say a larger unit keeps permanently its working maps, what's your definition of a larger unit?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a basic tactical unit is a battalion, and associated tactical units are brigades, regiments, divisions which have a corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... will have got -- Delic's unit and any group of battalion size, at least, on your evidence, should have retained working maps on a permanent basis, showing where things were actually -- where units were actually deployed, shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what it means. You didn't understand me again. A battalion, let me repeat for the third time: Once an assignment has been carried out, an analysis has been carried out it, it destroys the working map by burning it. A joint tactical unit, such as regiments, brigades, and divisions store their documents on a permanent basis. I apologise but my speech has become slurred. I'm swallowing my vowels so maybe the interpreters found it difficult to understand what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I understood your answer, at the very least a brigade will have retain permanent working maps showing where people were deployed, and that would be a contemporaneous document, won't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, after this we are going to adjourn in light of the witness's health problems. Answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That does not mean that the brigade will store it permanently. The brigade will hand over that map to the archives to be archived. Of course if it survived the bombing. And then the map will be permanently stored in the military archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it has been saved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So maps handed over would have been archived, working maps; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those that were handed over must be in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see those maps before you responded to the commission's request that you should provide statements?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see those maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any reason why those maps should not have been made available to the Office of the Prosecution by the commission, that you can think of?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't think of any reason, because I don't know whether they exist in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have no reason to believe they don't exist, do you, Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're asking me an ambiguous question. I don't know whether they exist. They must have been done, but whether they were destroyed or archived, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, these little maps - I'm holding up one which is a Delic exhibit, tab 367, and is of Bela Crkva - these little maps, drawn for the commission, are inevitably second best. Even if honest, these maps would be second best to the contemporaneously drawn working map held in an archive. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two things cannot be compared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us have just a straight and direct answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a direct answer to this question about the maps would be that these maps were made in end 2002, when the statements were given to the Commission for Cooperation with the ICTY. But I don't understand what he's asking me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's asking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because this is not a combat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just ask the question. He's asking whether you accept that these maps are second best to the contemporaneously drawn working maps that would be in the archives.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are not second best in terms of quality, but these maps are not a combat document. They were part of the statements, whereas the contemporaneous maps are combat documents. And I suppose contemporaneous documents are of greater value to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's an obvious answer, and when you were given no escape it was one you had to give, wasn't it? You've been trying to avoid the obvious answers throughout your testimony, Mr. Vukovic, haven't you, because you're not telling us the truth.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true at all. I'm telling the truth. But you cannot compare any map with a combat document. They're not in the same league. That's what I'm trying to say. They're absolutely not in the same league, in the same category. And a map that was done as a combat document contemporaneously has greater importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Court would like to go to the further of the two documents I've produced this morning to clear up the error, as I believe it to be, on the 27th of March. I've placed, or got Mr. Nort to place, on the overhead projector highlighted, I think, in, curiously enough, orange, I think, actually, the passage for the 27th of March from his diary, and it's been very difficult to decipher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you please, Mr. Vukovic, read this entry and we will follow the orange box, third from the top on the map I produced this morning to see where the error occurs. Can you read the entry out, please.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's for the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Linkage effected among all groups, meaning combat groups, by 0700 hours. At 0930, cleaning began in three directions. First group Major Sel, axis Donje Retimlje, trig point 356, Neprebiste village. Second group, Staff Sergeant First Class Ilijevski, village Zojic, Medvedce, Mamusa village. Third group, Lieutenant Radojevic in blockade in the stream."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The error would appear to be Medvedce as opposed to Medregovac, and subject to that correction, I would invite the Chamber to find this document a useful document and to perhaps admit it into exhibit, both of them. I have one more question to ask the witness about them and it's this:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You understood perfectly well, I must suggest to you, Mr. Vukovic, when you started your long answer about inaccuracies of the map and everything else, you understood perfectly well that what the Prosecution had done on this map was to try to reflect in a visually comprehensible way what is shown on your contemporaneous documentation. As a military officer reaching the rank of colonel, you must have understood that that's what we were trying to demonstrate. Yes?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you are trying to do, and I will answer why you are not correct, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've given your answers on errors as you allege them to be already. Likewise, in the other map which picks up from contemporaneous Delic documents, the Prosecution has set out in a visually comprehensible way the position of his troops according to his diary on the given dates. You understand that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, if it's true, because I didn't read General Delic's diary, who was a colonel then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These maps, these schematic maps, turned into visual aids as they have been, seek to provide the information that should be available in one format or another on the archived working maps that we have not been provided with. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying. Most of those positions as drawn in are correct. At that time, part of the units were also in those places, although it's not completely precise. But for the most part. It does coincide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And none of the maps, in particular these little maps produced for the commission, but none of the maps produced show anything about activity. At best, they purport to show static position of troops. They don't actually show anything about what happened, do they?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. Maybe they don't show it to you, but they show it to every soldier. If we put any of these maps on the overhead projector, I'll demonstrate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You take one and show me how it shows what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you choose or will you let me choose?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Choose one. You offered. You make your choice.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take this one, for instance. They're all the same, but here's one. This is the map of Retimlje for the 26th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say first of all that this map was accompanied by a set of statements of the greatest part of officers who on this date, the 26th of March, 1999, were in the field here in this area, and it's an integral part of the statements. To every soldier --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and this map was planned for the expert team, the following is visible -- sorry, I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you got all those statements? You said it was by the greatest part of officers who were in the field area and you've gone on to say something about the expert team. Have we got all the statements?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you received them. How can I know that? I have a great number of statements of my subordinates, which I can give you for your consideration. I received them during proofing, and I know that all commanders of combat groups provided statements and that a great number of platoon commanders and company commanders also gave statements, because I see those men regularly, and among other things they told me that they had given statements. But let me come back to the map. Here you see static units in the blockade line. It says in the left bottom corner, "blocking forces." And those forces do not move throughout the duration of the action. All the other forces are shown as they were in -- at 1600 hours. Green is the police. You see -- you see the position at 600 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 600 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then you see the position at 1200 hours. You see a double line, one of which is yellow, which tells everyone that this unit here moved from 6 to 12 up to here. Everybody who knows anything about it understands that if a unit moves less than one kilometre from 6.00 to 12.00, it must have been exposed to strong fire, in this case by terrorists, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a minute. "Must have been exposed to strong fire." Is that marked on the map? Is the fact of combat marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, this is not a working map. This is an integral part of the statements and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... question, because you're not allowed just to go on indefinitely. It doesn't show it on this map. Before we lose the point, is the fact that that unit was compelled to move by, as you would say, force, is that shown in your diary? Is it going to be shown in your combat records, your daily combat records? Or is this an assertion of yours that has no support in a contemporaneous document? You tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my combat report you were able to read that by the end of the day the unit had executed such-and-such a task and taken up such-and-such a line. Do you really expect me to record from rock to rock where every soldier went? As for action and fire, you see the action of the Siptar unit which, regrettably, managed to break through towards Dobrodeljane and later Mount Milanovac. That's why the anti-terrorist action in this terrain took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A very simple question, to which a very simple answer is possible: Is there any contemporaneous recording of your suggestion that this unit moved as a result of, as you describe it, Siptar action? Yes or no. We've got your entry for the 26th of March, if you want to look at it, in the diary.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my diary, it's not there, but it exists. It's part of the analysis of this anti-terrorist action that has been executed. It was introduced as number 4. Let me check. I'll tell you exactly which number it is. It's number 5, actually, in my set. And if you look carefully at the analysis, you will see all parts of the action; the disposition of the terrorists, our activities, all movements by axes, by hour, by day. And you will see --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the action of NATO aviation for cluster bombs at 1302 -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One thing at a time. It may be there. I'm not challenging that it's there, I just want to find it. Just read out the bit that deals with the movement of this group.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will find it for you. Give me just a second, because I'm not very good at finding my way around through these papers. There are many of them. To make this understandable, I'll start from the beginning, from point 1. Should I put it on the overhead projector?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just find us the bit that deals with the movement of this unit. It may be there at Retimlje on the 26th of March, so that we can that there's a, in this case it would be a near contemporaneous account, the fact that they moved under Siptar terrorist force, if that's what the position is. That's what I want you to help me with. You've told us it's there. It may be. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on page 2. In point 2. One, two, three, four, five, sixth paragraph. Although this, Mr. Nice, is part of a whole that goes together with point 1, which speaks of Siptar terrorist forces, but you can see it also from here. Do you want me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the course of the second day of combat operations, Siptar terrorist forces were broken up, crushed. Village Randubrava was captured, and the 23rd Detachment emerged in the wide area of Brestovac slopes. Control was taken of Retimlje village, and in Retimlje village, incidentally, there was a headquarters of Siptar terrorist forces. Opterusa, Samodreza and Studencani village were also taken control of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What are you looking at? What's the tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 359, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's number 5 in my set. It's the analysis of operations by the 549th Motorised Brigade in the destruction of Siptar terrorist forces in the broader area of Retimlje, and the blocking of Suva Reka-Orahovac road, dated 30th March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's Delic tab 359. 359 Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The characteristic of combat operations on day two was decisive defence against the remnants of the Siptar terrorist forces, the pull-out of forces into Neprebiste and Mamusa villages, and the linkage of our forces, Combat Groups 5 and 6, along the road Orahovac-Suva Reka. You can see that on the map. Which penned in the Siptar terrorist forces that remained in valleys and the villages of Mamusa and Medvedce. At dusk our forces linked up again to prevent the remaining Siptar terrorist forces from withdrawing. And then it follows to describe day three of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... day two. So the detail isn't there. It's a generalised account, there is no detail. The working map might have shown the detail, mightn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All these details were drawn into the working map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm not, obviously, in a position to deal with a whole sheaf of other statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many statements do you say you got from your commanders to deal with, for example, Retimlje? How many statements were made available to you by the commission?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the commission that made available any statements to me. I stated that part of the statements by my subordinates were given to me here during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was shown the statements of my subordinates. I have them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count them, I can count them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well you better have a look. You better count them and give us the names of them. I suppose it's going to take some time, but it's necessary. So you came here, you were given the witness statements or statements of other people, you read those, and in giving your evidence you're telling us, in part, what they said. Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the truth. I testified solely on the basis of my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And my statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was written on the basis of commanders from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... do you? Why bother to look at the other people's statements?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the same reason for which I read this disgusting book that you produced as a document, for the same reason that I read the rules of the service, although I know it by heart, almost, because I taught it for nine years --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the military academy. But out of respect for this Court, I took the trouble to prepare. For the same reason for which I looked at every document on the basis of which I was supposed to testify; to check once again whether my knowledge is correct. I will produce them for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... names of the people whose statements you've read. We'll see if they're statements we've seen ourselves already.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll be reading them order: Staff Sergeant First Class Ilijevski Oliver. In this anti-terrorist action, he commanded a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that you have asked for?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I just want to know the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just the names, not the contents of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milovan Zivkovic. I would not like to read the next name because this man may have problems. His family is in Kosovo and Metohija. If you really want to hear it, I would like to do it in private session. Oliver Ilijevski again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major Jan Sel, yes. Next?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Janos Sel. Then again Oliver Ilijevski. Let me see if there's any other name. It's mainly the same officers who took part in this anti-terrorist action together with me. Yes, it's their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think -- I can't remember all the names of the commission statements that have been offered for consideration. I don't think all of those names -- some of them are familiar but I don't think all of them. My observations on the unsatisfactory nature of witnesses coming to give evidence being provided with the statements of others are all too obvious to make. I'm going to press on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you look now, please, at one other map. To save you the time, I'll give you my copy of it and put it on the overhead projector. It's tab -- tab 361 of Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While it is being prepared, Mr. Nice, just for clarification, did we not see some of the working maps when Delic was here? I think several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We may have seen one or two but I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we heard the explanation from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That I'm afraid I cannot remember now, but Your Honour has probably got it in mind straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have found it in LiveNote. Shall I cite it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Tab 204, General, the working map. 'This is also the commander's working map ..." et cetera. "Yes. This is my working map. It is signed by me. And this was also something that my security officer kept updated. ... And these are activities of the army, of the MUP, and activities against civilians." Et cetera. It's on day 391, page 37, from line 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's an earlier period, I think, because it was tab 204.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are tabs 18, 128, 151, 204, 487 are working maps, according to my research.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, unless I'm mistaken, none of them cover this period of time, they are all surrounding this period of time, but I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The recent one, 487 is dated April sometime 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, surprisingly, nothing for the period of March. Or not surprisingly, perhaps explicably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just look at this one, which is Bela Crkva. This again is a produced map purporting to show the disposition of troops at a fixed moment in time at 0600 hours, and according to this map nobody is in Bela Crkva of any -- no troops, no police, nothing is in Bela Crkva; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's no other map produced by you or by anyone else that shows the disposition of police or the military in Bela Crkva, is there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I did not produce any such thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Previous people --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but how can I know whether somebody else did?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course the learned Trial Chamber Judges will have to decide what happened in Bela Crkva, but it's clear that if things happened in Bela Crkva at the hands of police and the military then there is no document, no contemporaneous document that you've produced or to which you can refer that reveals what it was they did, because this is the best we've got. Is that right? This is the best we've got, and this isn't contemporaneous. This was made years later and this purports to show the disposition of troops at Bela Crkva. It doesn't show anything about what people were doing in Bela Crkva, anything. Hmm? This is the best we've got.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing can be seen on this map because there had been no action. That's what I've kept telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the only thing we've got --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards -- well, you've put another question to me. Please wait for me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on you're going say that I did not respond. You told me that I did not bring a single contemporaneous document which confirms action or non-action in a particular village, and I keep telling you here are the documents that are contemporaneous. This is the most reliable of all, the analysis of the action taken. Can you find a more reliable document than this? And yet you're unwilling to accept it. Here you can see that there was no action in Bela Crkva. Had there been any action, it would have been recorded in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... map back. The most, I must suggest to you, Mr. Vukovic, that there is one and only one reliable contemporaneous document that you've produced about Bela Crkva and it's your own diary which sets out in clear and unequivocal terms that Bela Crkva was cleansed, a document written on and for the 25th of March, and that's exactly what you and your troops were doing, cleansing this area of people. Yes?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn to Mala Krusa -- sorry, Velika Krusa. You made an observation about how the evidence produced was unreliable. It's a little ambiguous in the transcript because you say the man should have shown his burns or we should have brought the man here who was burned in that awful incident if it was true. Can you explain what you were saying? It may not be your fault, it may be the translation or -- may be a possibility of translation error. What was it you were saying about producing somebody who was burned in the event at Krusa?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously it was not interpreted to you properly. I remember that question put by Mr. Milosevic. I can even find it in the questions. If necessary, I can quote it verbatim, but at any rate, even without the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can find it in the questions? What have you got there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I got a list of tentative questions that Mr. Milosevic is going to examine me about, a list of topics and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that the notes that you had that you were referring to that we didn't see you were looking at?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. These are not notes. Notes are this, and they're still on my desk. I know that I have to ask for permission if I wish to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was this question that you recalled being prepared to answer and what was the answer you intended to give and to convey? Hmm?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave my answer. And these are the questions on the basis of which I prepared myself in preparation for the testimony. First there were the broader topics, and then within each topic there were certain questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that I would be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... please.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I've been trying to tell you. I remember that question during the examination-in-chief, and it is not said that he was burned, but that a large group of civilians were allegedly brought into a house which was then covered with gasoline and straw, and then, if I remember correctly, they first shot at them and then torched them. And this witness happens to be the only survivor. That's the way it's put in the indictment. And later on, he stated to some witness who testified here about how all of this had happened. In my answer, I put a question, a logical question: Why didn't he come, then, to testify if such a person exists? I expressed my doubts as to whether such a person existed at all. I did not say that somebody who got killed should come in and testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You made an observation about a man, but just have a look at this picture, please. In fact, there were several survivors of this incident. We called one or two before the Trial Judges, but if you look at this man. This is a man by the name of Selami Elshani, who was so badly burned he could see parts of his flesh falling off him as he ran away, and he gave an interview for and was recorded giving an account of this event in the autumn of 1999 on a BBC Panorama programme. Two points: Do you say there was no such incident of people being shot and then burnt in Velika Krusa? Do you say it didn't happen at all? Hmm?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke properly when I said that it is certain that my soldiers did not do this, and I don't have any knowledge of any other unit or soldiers having done something like that. Whether something like that happened or not is such a hypothetical question that I really cannot answer it either by a yes or a no. I don't have any knowledge of any such thing. If I had such knowledge, I'd tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember that you've been given many opportunities by the Court and by me to say, "Well, I don't know about something happening but it may have happened at the hands of someone else." Now, do you allow for the possibility that this terrible, terrible massacre may have happened at the hands of police officers?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I have not come here to guess. I can just testify and tell the truth, because among other things, I am bound to do that by the solemn declaration I made here. I really don't want to engage in guesswork.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that this event, which is laid largely at the door of the police but with support, I think, from the Serb military outside the village, the subject of many witnesses' evidence and a great deal of public writings, do you accept that this incident may have happened?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to answer this question, because you are not putting a specific question. I am telling you that war itself is a crime. Now, whether there were individual cases, probably there were. There are in any war. If you're asking me if such a thing had been organised, I'm saying no to you, because in order for something to be organised, there has to be an order. I'd have to know, as commander of a unit, that such an order had existed, had it existed. If you read carefully the order of the brigade commander for this action, you will see the procedure --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you just answer my question. We've spent so much time with your long answers. Do you accept that this may have happened? Yes or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. no.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that it may have happened and that individuals who got out of control could have done it, but I don't have any knowledge as to any such thing having happened, so I cannot say either yes or no to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In light of that final concession, why is it when the accused asked you about this at 12.46 on day 431 of this trial that you asserted without equivocation that everything said about this appalling massacre was -- none of it was true, you said, and there were untruths contained in it, and then you gave your explanation and made reference to not seeing a burnt man. Why did you give that evidence when it was simply not within your knowledge or power to do so, Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had excellent knowledge. And in that case I was answering a concrete question, whereas you are not putting a concrete question. You're asking me whether I allow for a possibility or not. You're not asking me whether my unit did it or whether I have knowledge about this event. Mr. Milosevic asked me very specifically about this event, and I gave a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Nice, what the question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What actually led to your answer, Mr. Vukovic, was a recitation by the accused of some of the evidence of a witness called Ali Hoti. The accused said to you on the 29th of March, Mehmet Krasniqi told him that on a day in Mala Krusa the Serbian police and paramilitaries rounded up 109 men, including this Krasniqi, took them to a house, covered them with straw, poured petrol on them and set fire to them. This Krasniqi survived somehow, so Ali Hoti learnt this from this Krasniqi man. You then, without being asked a question, volunteered by interruption of the flow of words from the accused: "All I can say is that none of this is true. There are several untruths in it." And you then went on to give an answer about paramilitaries, and you said, "Why didn't this Krasniqi come to show the burns?" You weren't asked a direct question. You volunteered that this information, recited as evidence by the accused, was false. Had the accused given you a question, had you written down a question from him that you were going to answer at this stage?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, what you're saying is not right. You yourself said that I was commenting on allegations contained in the question, and I assume that these are allegations from the indictment, and I said why each and every allegation was wrong. I talked about paramilitary formations, which I never saw in my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please listen to the question. What was put to you was what a witness said in this court, not words of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's right, and I commented on the allegations made by that witness, and I said that they were not truthful. As soon as he mentions paramilitary formations, I know that the rest is not true because there couldn't have been any paramilitary formations and there weren't any paramilitary formations in the zone of responsibility of the 549th Brigade. I can guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where, of course, locally armed Serbs dressed in a range of different uniforms which might well have appeared to be paramilitaries, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All of those who were armed had to have either a regular police uniform or an army uniform and clear insignia on the sleeves of the uniform and on the cap, beret, or helmet, depending on what they wore. And they also had to have rank insignia if they held a rank, if they were officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
