utterances.text: Some of them had white ribbons on their arms, as the evidence reveals.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of ribbons you're talking about. White ones? As far as I can remember, no. Sometimes we wore red bands, but they were worn on shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... as indeed appears in Delic's instructions, locally armed Serbs were used in this operation, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that information. Possibly, but they were under the command of the military, of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you seek an answer to the question about whether this was one of a list of questions provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I do, actually. I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this question about the Mala Krusa incident subject of a question -- was this question about the Mala Krusa incident prepared by the accused for you to answer? Was it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the questions. He showed me statements made by Prosecution witnesses, and he asked me to answer that question during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were prepared to do so despite the fact that, as you finally revealed to the Court, there is no way you can exclude the possibility that this appalling event happened in the way survivors described, is there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Then and now I'm giving the same answer. I don't know how you find a difference in my answer. After all, I am prepared to give you all the other questions or, rather, give answers to all the questions again if you put them to me. I have would have come here as a Prosecution witness, too, had you called me, but you did not call me. Obviously, you don't want to hear what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, just for the avoidance of any doubt in your mind about whether or not your position has been consistent, you said even today that you doubted the existence of such a burned person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you still doubt the existence of such a burned person? You've seen the picture of this one.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to express my doubt because this picture doesn't mean anything to me. It could have been taken anywhere or at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Perhaps we can just look at -- if Mr. Nort would be good enough, just see what he actually said about it. It's in English but I've actually got a B/C/S version for you, so you can have that as well. He happened not to have been called, but since you asked about a burned person, you shall have the chance to see what he said. That can go on the overhead projector, and that for the witness to follow, and I'll follow on the overhead projector. Thank you. I hope I've got the right one. Handwritten version signed by the wife of the person concerned. See, this man, I'll take it swiftly because we -- top of the page, please, thank you. His name is Selami Elshani. Do you follow it? He went to Krushe e Mahdi, stayed with his mother's brother. There was small KLA presence in the village. Then he describes how on the 25th of March the shelling of Krushe e Madhi began with all sorts of military pieces, as he describes it. He then describes how --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. I cannot follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He then describes how first of all the VJ shelled the village to open the way for the police infantry to carry out attacks. "These police wore uniforms similar to those of the VJ; greenish camouflage combat uniform with 'Policija' in large letters on the right epaulet. They wore a white ribbon. They also wore body armour. They carried rocket launchers, pistols and Kalashnikovs. The shelling lasted from 4.30 or 5.00 on Thursday the 25th of March ..." Then further down the page, you'll have to skip just to save time, he deals with a speech by Seselj which was inciting violence, and then he comes to the 26th, and he says: "At about 300 hours on the 26th --" have you found that point, please? "At about 300 hours on the 26th --"

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. "We were completely surrounded by tanks of the VJ driven by people in police uniforms. I base this on earlier experience. There were armoured cars from the VJ. The police walked to the gully where they were and fired shots in the air." Then the next sentence: "At 0500 we were forced to surrender. None of us was armed." He then deals with the circumstances of their search. He deals with the sending of women and children to the mosque. He deals with the burning of all personal identification papers. Next page, please, Mr. Nort. And I'll find you the relevant point, please. Top of the page, please. Top of the page so I can read it. Thank you very much. He deals with a particular couple of men who were photographed with an Albanian flag. And then he says this -- see if you can find this point: "The police spoke in Serbian and got more angry when the two men couldn't answer them because they couldn't understand. These young men were left there."

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot follow this any longer. I don't know which line you've reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you can find the figure 200 men, in figures, you'll be at the right place.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the sentence or so before that it says: "These young men were left there. The pictures were torn up. And in Serbian they said 'You will pay for this later.' I don't know the names of these young men. They then herded us to a yard in a village where we, the 200 men, were made to lie face down with our fingers locked behind our heads. We were left like that for five hours. They beat us with sticks from time to time." Next sentence deals with how he was attacked, divided into three groups, told all those not from this village to step forward. Fifteen of them did. And then the next sentence begins: "The remainder were divided into two, the younger ones, under 60 and the older ones over 60 years approximately. My group was herded to a derelict house 30 to 40 metres away." Next sentence but one: "They said no, that allegedly we had asked NATO to come and shell them and because of this, they were going to execute us. They told us to ask Bill Clinton to help us. We realised they really were going to execute us. We asked for a few drops of water at the moment of our departure of life -- from life. This last request was rejected." He goes on in the next -- he describes the room and then he explains how one of the five policemen said, "Let's begin with the execution of them." "We were huddled together in a corner. I was nearest to the policeman. After the first shot, I threw myself to the ground and I acted as if I was dead. I was on my back. One by one the others began to fall on top of me. They started with single shots and then with automatic fire. They had Kalashnikovs. Their blood was dripping on my face, and as I lay there, a bullet grazed my left shoulder and cut just the skin. Everyone was dead. No one moved a single muscle. The shooting lasted about 30 seconds but it felt like an hour. I was so scared. I heard one of the policemen saying, 'While we cover them with cornstacks, you go and get some benzine.' They soaked us with the benzine. I could hear it pouring and could smell it. Then they set it alight. I wasn't sure if they were still there but I had to do something. I pushed the person on top of me aside and began to brush the flames aside with my bare hands. Both hands and my face were burnt. I stood on my knees and screamed with all my strength. I tried once more and managed to get away from the flames. I was lucky to have so many clothes on, otherwise I would have been completely burnt. I quickly began to undress. I had a plastic jacket on, which began to melt. As I did this, the skin and flesh began to fall off my hands." Then deals with his escape. That's what the burned man you said we should have brought said. Do you challenge that that account is true?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, the first part is false. And as soon as somebody starts lying, then he lies all the way through. Find the first page, where it says witness statement. It's towards the end. It says that on the 6th of March they were completely surrounded by tanks of the army of Yugoslavia that were driven by men in police uniforms. Well, this is a really bad lie, Mr. Nice. In combat action, no one from the outside can see who is in a tank because everybody is hidden and covered. So even if a person saw a tank, he could not see the person in the tank. What did he say here? Just a moment. Let me find this. They were driven by men in police uniforms, and he bases that on some kind of previous experience. This is a complete lie. Further on, there were armoured vehicles of the VJ, et cetera. And I'm telling you that in this area I was the only one who had tanks, and I know that my tanks were not in Velika Krusa. This unit that you can see, if we look at the map again, the one that you see on the asphalt road Djakovica-Prizren, did not move on any one of those three days. After all, that was the assignment it had received in the relevant order. It did not move. Now you have confirmed my belief that this witness is lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether he is really on that photograph or not is something that I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are at the end of the one-hour session. We will adjourn for 20 minutes -- for 15 minutes, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The -- you've now firmed up your position, have you, that this burnt man is simply lying in his statement. Is that your position? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of the statement he made that he had seen the men in the tank. And I tell you that that is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've all seen pictures of people in tanks, both with the hatch where the driver sits being open and with people standing on the top of the tank where their uniforms can be seen. Is there something different about your tanks from the tanks we've all seen like that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the weaponry of the army of Yugoslavia has two types of tanks or, rather, there is a third type, too, which is a modification of the others. They're similar, but in every tank in a combat action the crew of a tank, the men manning the tank, are inside the tank, and for their protection everything is closed, the hatches are closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, when a tank is visiting an area of civilians that it wishes to terrorise, it doesn't necessarily have to be in readiness for combat action. These tanks were going to terrorise and drive out civilians. So think back. It's possible, isn't it, that people can be seen on the top of the tank or indeed with the hatch open? Hmm?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not so. And those tanks weren't going to terrorise the population, because I kept them under my immediate control and command throughout, and they were never given to the police. And find me one policeman who was capable of driving a tank, as your witness said. And find me any policeman or a single policeman who knows how to use a firing gun and communication within a tank, the aiming device and communication devices. You go to school for that, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... your attention -- I drew to your attention the statement of the burned man because you raised it, but there are two other witnesses, Lufti Ramadani and Mehmet Avdyli, both of whom described to this Court Serb tanks coming to this village, firing on the men, throwing hay on the bodies, putting gasoline on top and setting fire to it. Is it your case that these people are all untrue or would you like to go back to your earlier answer and allow for the possibility that this event did happen? Hmm?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't allow for the possibility of tanks and armoured vehicles being in the village of Velika Krusa from the 25th to the 28th of March, 1999. I don't allow for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just finish in this way with a few general questions that you may able to help us with. These people, the thousands of them that left in those few days between the 26th and the 1st of April that we can see summarised on this document, they wouldn't have left, would they, but for the presence on this territory of your troops?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please be more precise. Left where; to Albania or their homes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They wouldn't have left their homes, in some cases, I suppose, if their homes hadn't been burnt, but for the generality of them, they wouldn't have left for Albania but for the presence on their homeland of your armed forces, would they?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Start from the beginning. The armed forces -- it is normal for the armed forces to be present in everybody's homeland, and the armed forces would not have arrived, specifically speaking, in any of these villages had there not already been terrorists in those villages. And as far as the departure to Albania is concerned, the basic course, as I've already said, was the NATO bombing. And specifically in this particular village. Nogavac was shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, your documents don't show that. Your documents show that, for the most part, like Bela Crkva, these villages didn't have KLA in them. One or two were said to have some, but most of these villages on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which your tanks went according -- and cleansed didn't have KLA. Let's go back to my question. These people wouldn't have moved but for the presence of your troops, would they? It's very simple and it's very obvious, I suggest to you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is very simple, but you first of all made an observation with which I do not agree. So you keep saying and -- you are persistent in saying that the army was in villages where there were no terrorists, and I say the opposite, that the army went into action only in those villages from which the terrorists shot at the army or were present there. Now, as far as the movement of civilians is concerned, it is quite normal that before the beginning of an operation the civilian population leaves the area where combat operations were taking place. Find me one civilian, one man who is not afraid of losing his life and of having his children lose their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you were only a -- I don't say that offensively, but you were a colonel. Why launch this campaign on the 25th of March? Why not do it in February or January if it had something to do with the KLA? Why wait for the cover of NATO? Hmm?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand that observation that I'm only a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me make it simple for you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But anyway, as far as the rest of the question goes, why we launched it then, we launched it then because, according to the assessments of the corps command, the Pristina Corps command and the assessments of the brigade command, strong terrorist forces had appeared in that area. And that's what it says in both orders, that they had cut across the -- or cut off the communication line that was of vital importance for supplies to the army coming in, in-depth, and that is why we looked at both orders in order to deblock certain communication lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was purely --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we also conducted operations in January and February, wherever the terrorists appeared and jeopardised communication lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... pure coincidence that it started at the time of the NATO bombing, is it? Pure coincidence?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you take a look at the order issued and the documents from the relevant period, they were compiled before the aggression started. Don't call it a campaign, it was an aggression against a sovereign country. So you will see that it says the brigade command, it wrote its order on the 23rd of March, 1999, and let me remind you that the aggression started at 1900 hours, or 1959, on the 24th of March. So the decisions were made that this be done on the basis of valid information and data and on the basis of experience gained on the terrain prior to the aggression, before the aggression of the NATO countries started. I don't want to mention them all: France, Albania, and all the other countries that took part. And this can be seen from the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that the plan was dated the 23rd of March. That may be dated that, but just as a matter of detail --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it is. Not possible, but that's how it is, and that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The plan, you see, as a matter of interest, you said it was planned on the 23rd. Is this something you'd have expected to see reflected in the Supreme Defence Council meetings, given the scale of the plan? Hmm?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was an operation -- well, not an operation, an action, an anti-terrorist action with a joint composition of men. If you look at the forces, you will see that about 800 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You'd expect to this reflected in the Supreme Defence Council, wouldn't you? Coming from the Commander-in-Chief and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At all events I don't expect the Supreme Commander, Commander-in-Chief to deal with individual anti-terrorist actions. He probably issued some directive in 1998, as far back as 1998, that wherever terrorist forces are found action should be taken against them. And this was a combat disposition in the area of responsibility of a brigade commander. So quite naturally, he acted within the spirit of previously issued orders and assignments. I can't claim that, but it wasn't the level that would go to the Supreme Defence Council to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can help us, Your Honour, but the very last document we've been provided with is an SDC record of the 23rd of March, thereafter it being denied that such records exist in one form or another, either as SDC records or as Joint Command records, and there is no higher level document dealing with this plan at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Isn't the position quite simply this, Mr. Vukovic, that this campaign, which actually starts, as we see, on the 25th of March, was built on the prospect that the bombing wouldn't last very long and there was a short period of time in which you could kick out some Albanians, and that's what you did?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's not what was done. Allow me to finish, please. Allow me to finish my answer to your question. So this was not a campaign. Let me repeat for the hundredth time, this was an anti-terrorist action. And quite naturally, it is quite natural for the armed forces to fight against terrorists as they do in all normal countries throughout the world, with all available resources. And I don't know why this isn't clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you and all the other officers and so on who have been providing statements to and through the VJ commission have been doing that which you gave away by your observation where you said there was different interpretation of events. You've been trying to put together a dishonest, perjurious story to mislead this Court, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't remember all the things you said. You've uttered quite a number of untruths, but I'll try and address each of the individual areas. First of all, we did not reach any kind of agreement or pool our forces. And you mentioned officers, but I'm going to speak in my own name. I did not have any doubts, Mr. Nice. The doubts were on the part of the commission, I assume, which was given the task of investigating and studying -- well, I'm starting to assume now, make my own assumptions because I don't know for sure what it did, but I was never in any doubt myself because I know exactly what happened over there. I know exactly what my army, my soldiers, did there, and you can feel free to bring in all 186 of my soldiers if you like - I apologise, 185, because I was the one 186th - and they will confirm what I've told you. And of course everybody will be speaking from their own level because a soldier can see 20 to 30 metres to the left or right of him and in front of him, each soldier. So I do not agree with what you said at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: However coarsened may have been sensitivities in the time of this conflict, at the time coarsened, you've all realised since that in signing your name, as you've done in your diary, to cleansing the area, you are implicated in these terrible crimes and that's why you're having to come and lie and lie again to this Court.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is just not true, and you have insulted me again, Mr. Nice, and told me that I'm lying. As I have been forbidden to say that you are lying, to tell you that you're lying, then all I'm going to say is that you're not telling the truth, that you're telling untruths. But in fact I think that you're lying but I'm not allowed to say that publicly. And it is not true that I committed any crime, that I am implicated in any way, as you have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, I spoke to you about that. It's a distinction between the professional and the personal. I explained to you that Mr. Nice, when he says you are lying, is not speaking from a personal point of view. He's putting his case. He does so on the basis of instructions and the statements that he has, and that is why he can put to you, and it is quite normal in the adversarial system for counsel to put to a witness that he's lying, but it is wholly improper for you to say that Mr. Nice is lying. You must refrain from that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, I didn't say he was lying. I said he did not -- was not telling the truth. He was telling an untruth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Mr. Robinson. I shall do my best to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice -- I'm sorry, Mr. Milosevic. Let us deal with the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I should have. I've only, I think, produced four new documents, the two maps, the statement of the man of Elshani and his photograph. Dealing with -- I haven't said I produced, the only things I've shown that are new, I think, are those. Well, there's the visual aid that I put right at the beginning but that's the same as the visual aid that was used with Delic, and I don't know what state that occupies at the moment, but I'm happy for it to be exhibited and indeed would urge that it be exhibited because it's a very useful summary of material found elsewhere, and if it's an exhibit then it's available for use in argument without it being in any way proposed as a document that is itself evidence; it simply summarises material elsewhere. Likewise, these two maps we've produced overnight I would urge the Trial Chamber to admit as exhibits. The witness has to an extent finally acknowledged that they accurately reflect entries found elsewhere. First the entries in his own documents and, secondly, entries if they are established, and we can deal with that when the Delic diary is available in translation, from the Delic diary. They're valuable because, as we now know, documents of the same generic kind as this apparently exist, or certainly existed but presumably still exist, and have been denied to us, and these are more useful documents than the confusing maps which have static positions placed on them and don't actually reveal anything of the activity of the troops, because these maps don't. So I'd urge these documents to be admitted. As to the statement of the man Elshani and his photograph, I would ask the Chamber on this occasion to accept it as evidence. Of course we didn't, in the event, call that man. We called two or three others, but it was this witness who chose to challenge the calling of people who were burned. And although I think one of our witnesses himself had been burned, this is a striking example of a person seriously burned and of his accompanying statement, and I'd ask the Chamber to say that this can all be admitted as useful in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would be your position in relation to The Traces of Inhumanity and the recorded conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I made my position clear this morning that I am no position to accept or reject it. I hope that I will have the resources to make some further inquiries into the tape or the recording of the tape. The Court's point made by His Honour Judge Kwon is obviously a valid one for argument; namely, that the witness could or should have brought in the tape itself, but if he's right and if we find in answer to perhaps His Honour Judge Bonomy's point this morning that there are other sources that have given the same tape, we can deal with that matter maybe by admission. If not, then it might be thought preferable not for that document to be exhibited at the moment. I suspect generally it falls within the category of material that witnesses are allowed to produce subject to the exercise of discretion by the Court, but this is such an extreme example, going to show particular animus on the part of NATO that without better support it might be thought lacking indicia of reliability sufficient to justify its inclusion as evidence, but I will make the efforts that I've spoken of to try and see if we can confirm its accuracy or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And one clarification in regard to this map this, marked map. The strongholds here, are those places marked by -- indicated the by this witness or it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He accepted yesterday, if you remember, when I put the names of these places to him as KLA strongholds, he accepted that I was more or less right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He also mentioned, for example, Randubrava and Retimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right, he mentioned Retmilje and other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right, there is nothing to stop those being marked, in addition, or simply the subject of memory, but he certainly accepted in general terms that the blue rectangles showed areas of KLA strength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope you heard the witness explaining that these maps, according to what they show, are rather distorted. He commented the map you provided on the basis of General Delic's diary, and he said that places are mentioned -- when places are mentioned, it -- they were in fact regions, much broader areas, regions around those places, whereas here, the points were the dots showed places and every military document mentions axes like Bela Crkva-Retimlje, that axis. It doesn't mean that the army is only in Bela Crkva or Retimlje, but it refers to a direction, an axis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does that not go more to the weight than the admissibility of the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, the weight of them. And the witness agreed and testified that his units were in these places that are marked. However, there too there was a certain amount of distortion because the map showed, according to the legend provided, that the blue squares were the KLA strongholds, as if they were not strongholds where the red, yellow, and orange squares were, and it appears, according to that, that the army attacked territory where there were no KLA strongholds and just went to the strongholds later on, which is not correct because the witness challenged that. So this map is incorrect, too, and cannot be taken as an argument. It can be taken as a graphic approach of where the army and soldiers were on any particular day. But it's quite clear from the statement made by the witness and from his testimony that most of these points, and as far as I remember at all of these points except Bela Crkva, there were KLA strongholds. So the yellow, orange, and red points, that there were KLA strongholds there and not just in the ones designated in blue. And then one more -- another comment that I'd like to make, remark. For example, in this square here where we have these remarks on the left-hand side, the vertical column, it says the forces ready to intervene along the Orahovac-Ostrozub axis, and then underneath that it says during the day 1.000 people left in the direction of Cafa Prusit. So when you combine the two you gain the impression that they left because the forces were moving along that axis, whereas these elements here were taken from the diary about the events that had taken place on that particular day, and the witness explained that in great detail, what -- how entries were made into a war diary. So these two events have nothing to do with each other, whereas Mr. Nice intentionally tries to gain the impression that they were linked up and that one followed on from the other, which is quite incorrect. And the witness did say that those citizens were from Pec and not from these areas at all where the action had taken place, those that were going on that day and passed by on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we note the arguments you have made against the admission of the two maps, but these are arguments that go more to the weight than the admissibility, and you can present those arguments against later -- those arguments again, at a later stage. We'll admit the two maps, one number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 930, tab 1, for the map reflecting entries in Vukovic's diary. Tab 2 is the map reflecting the entries in Delic's diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll not admit the statements, nor will we admit the photographs of the burned person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases. Ms. Dicklich reminds me that there's the potential for problem over the expanded documents originally coming in in a very limited form as tabs of this witness's exhibits, the diaries and the daily records. In each case, for him as well as for Djosan, we have obtained more complete versions of the originally selected documents and provided some translations. I -- my recollection is that with Djosan we substituted all the additional material for what was in the original tab. That was, I think, the Chamber's decision. I'm in your hands entirely as to what we should do with these other exhibits, but obviously there should be some reflection of the fact that we've put in the full documents and some parts in translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. As far as I remember, I produced these documents, not Mr. Nice, these full documents. I gave them to you before Colonel Vukovic started to testify. They were originals that were copied and then made available to Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the exercise of admission would be facilitated if you were to identify those parts that were utilised during evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It will take some time to deal with that as an exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I understand the tension between putting in everything, which then has to go off for translation at great burden to the institution as a whole, and identifying the selected passages. In relation to these documents, if we just look at them, it may be on this occasion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is such a waste of time. Can Mr. Kay and you not between you identify them and if you agree they can be filed through the -- or at least indicated to the Registry what's being substituted, and we can be told, and if you can't agree, you can bring it back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My only suggestion was going to be that on this occasion because the two additional diaries are comparatively slender, it might have been worth just putting them all in and having the translation of the parts we've got. So that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As I understood it, it was to be the parts that were used of the diary that were to be exhibited, and what I propose is that if we track that through the transcripts and then merge it into a single document that we file with a cover sheet to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, at the beginning of the examination, you were asked which documents you had available to you when you were giving your statement to the commission, which contemporaneous documents, and you identified three. Now I'm asking you, did you in your statement that you gave rely mainly on what was written in those documents or mainly on what you saw and heard with your own eyes and ears while you were on the ground and what you did with your unit?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, when I was giving the statements, I relied first and foremost on my own personal experience, and I used the documents available to me to confirm that, but during those four days, I was there in that area all the time in the disposition of my units, and I gave statements based on my experience, direct experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does your direct experience differ in any way from what you found in those contemporaneous documents?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be precise, my knowledge is best reflected in the analysis, because the first two documents, the order and the decision, can be said to be a plan for the anti-terrorist action, whereas the analysis followed immediately after the completion of the anti-terrorist action, and it was made, among other things, on the basis of the reports that I submitted to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. You have been shown some other sources here, including the book called "As Seen, As Told." You said that you read those parts of the book that relate to the area where you personally spent some time with your unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my first contact I read only that and copied only that. Later on, I read the rest of the book and I can comment on that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, tell us only this: Based on what you saw on the spot, and you are the only one in this room who was there on the spot in the critical days to which the book relates, what is correct about what you read, from what you read?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing is correct except that the army was present on the said dates in the said areas. Nothing of the rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that question as it appears relates to the whole book, you must see how ridiculous both the question and the answer are. Absolutely pointless.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand, Mr. Bonomy, this comment of yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness would have had to have been everywhere in Kosovo throughout the whole conflict to be able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said loud and clear, "Based on what you saw on the spot, [in English] and you are the only one in this room who was there on the spot in the critical days to which the book relates, what is correct about what you read?" [Interpretation] So I asked him about those places where he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you didn't. He told you that he had read the whole book, if you had been listening to his earlier answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard his previous answer, and I asked very precisely a question that relates to the places where he had been. He didn't ask a question of himself. I am asking the questions of him. So the question makes perfect sense. He was there, unlike all the rest of us, and he read sections of the book about the places where he had been, and I asked him what is correct about that. I asked him if there is a nucleus of truth in it, a grain of truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put another question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you can comment the book as a whole. What can you comment?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, briefly; I don't know how much time we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Only very briefly.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, if you look at page 152, it speaks of the position of religious leaders. I can put it on the overhead projector if that would be of assistance to the Trial Chamber. And I have to read a very, very short passage, if we have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have no -- I have no recollection of any question in cross-examination about religious leaders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were questions about the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly, Colonel. What is the point you're making about religious leaders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish to compare the way this book treats Orthodox priests with the way it treats Muslim and Catholic priests, and then it will be clear to you. Let me just tell you that I am a non-believer, an atheist. What the book says is this: "Religion plays a big role in the cultural identification of the Serbian nation and it was often used in the nationalist campaign of Serbian politicians from end 1980. From the viewpoint of the Serbian Orthodox Church, which appears on the public scene from the end of the communist era of the 1980s, its religious leaders suddenly found the means and the supporters necessary to re-establish their positions in society. That was the reason why they associated with forces --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not following at the same pace and the witness has just covered this passage with his hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you have to read a little more slowly, and don't cover the page with your hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. I'm trying to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Let the English version be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you repeat your reading where Velika Srbija appears. We didn't hear that interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "For this reason, they started to associate with ethnically divisive forces. The Serbian Orthodox Church backed Milosevic in his campaign for Greater Serbia from the beginning of the 1990s." I can read on because they said something about a later split, subsequent split. But in the next passage on the -- in the next column, it says: "As for the -- on the part of the Kosovo Albanian nation, religious identification was not particularly strong. Although most Kosovo Albanians are Muslim, there are Catholic and Orthodox Christian Kosovo Albanians." That's what it says here. Now, let me say what I wanted to. Anyone who has a modicum of knowledge about the events in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia knows the nature of the churches. It was -- it is precisely the Serbian Orthodox Church that was the most moderate, and it is the one that always appeals for peace, cooperation, tolerance. As for Islam, Islamic fundamentalism is known everywhere in the world as the greatest source of evil and terrorism. It has proven to be such in all other countries as well as in Kosovo and Metohija where units of the Mujahedin acted together with the KLA. I believe it is documented, although I myself haven't brought such a document, but I believe I can make it available to this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is the significance of the two passages for you, and we have had. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you go on, may I make it clear that I would never subscribe to the view that this witness is trying to express, if this is what he's saying, that all Muslims have to be feared because of their affinity with terrorism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I am sorry, I did not state that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do we have any need, Colonel, to dwell on this book any more? You told us what you knew, and you said that nothing in that book is correct apart from what you identified.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to be allowed to say that I was talking not about Muslims but about Islamic fundamentalism. I had many Muslims in my unit. We cooperated perfectly well, and I have absolutely no negative prejudice against that people. I only have negative things to say about Islamic fundamentalism and the jihad that supports terrorism. As for your question, I believe there is no need, but I can comment every single paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is no need to deal with the book any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Colonel, can I be clear on one other thing: Was this a subject that was part of the prepared questions given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, it was not, but please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- don't hold me to my word. But as far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were asked in cross-examination about one combat report. I believe it would be of assistance if you explained the following -- that's the big logbook of combat reports or, rather, daily reports that later turn into combat reports as the war began. Were they in fact recorded texts of messages that were sent as reports by radio?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The texts of both messages sent over the radio, and when the radio wasn't working the reports were sent via messenger. So these are the texts of the messages that were sent to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You were told during cross-examination that on the 24th of March, and you were also shown page 126 and you were asked to read that page, to confirm that there was no action or activity by Siptar terrorist forces on that day. That's on page 126 that was shown to you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find it. I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were told there was no mention of Siptar terrorist activities on that day. Please just read the last few lines of point 3.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads as follows: "Armed aggression carried out by NATO with the synchronised lighting of fires along the border of the Republic of Albania (which is how they marked the border of the Republic of Albania) in-depth spotlights were positioned in order to show certain mountains, et cetera." So there were no activities observed in my zone. Perenik [phoen] and Beli Drim were the boundaries of my zone on the north, but then there was Mount Milanovac, and on the other side there was the border in the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So activity was obvious on that day and recorded in this way in your diary.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, activity was observed and noticed on all days from the start of the aggression. There was synchronised, coordinated action between NATO forces in the air, and on the ground between the forces of Albania and the Siptar terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Further on you were shown the recording of the 26th of March, which is on page 127, and in 5.3, it says: "On the 27th ..." et cetera, and you were asked whether there is any mention of the names of these villages from Bela Crkva onwards, not to mention them all yet again. Now, please read 5.3.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads as follows: "On the 26th of March --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says the 27th of March here.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we're not talking about the same paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 127, it is the 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid we're not talking about the same document, then, because I haven't got it here that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The combat report?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got a complete one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The page was placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5.3 says: "On the 26th of March, 1999, the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade, on the in-depth security of the state border."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is also what I have in my document. But it's time for the break. We are going to adjourn for 15 minutes, and you can use the break to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- find the correct page you wish to refer to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have found it. I have it right in front of me and I just wish to say something to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you are reading out is correct, the 5.3 pertaining to the 26th of March, but please look on the right-hand side of that same page and you will see that the further entry is there, the 26th of March. It also has 5.3.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every combat report --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking can you see it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it. And 5.3 pertains to the proposal to engage units for further days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you about that after the break. I just wanted to direct your attention to where it was in the document.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 20 minutes -- for 15 minutes, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wish to clarify the question that Mr. Nice had put to you. For example, in this report for the 25th there is mention the 26th, why the 27th is mentioned of the report of the 26th. Actually, he didn't ask you about the next one, but you explained that it says on the 26th of March, of the 25th, we shall engage. So it is in the future tense.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, the future tense. It is a proposal to the Superior Command to engage forces for a task that was given in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Is that identical to what is on the right-hand side when it says for the following date, again there is a reference to Drina and these tasks. So the previous day includes the tasks were already given routinely in accordance with the previous order. Is that the gist of it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the gist of it. A day or two earlier, in advance, this order is given. And after all, if you look at the entire daily report, there is always the proposal for the engagement of forces for the days that will follow. That is in accordance with the orders of the command of the brigade when Combat Group 2 was established as far as back as 1998, and when we started carrying out tasks in the border area in terms of the in-depth security of the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're not going to dwell on that any longer. Please, Mr. Nice asked you about whether there was any civilian control or any kind of interference. I don't want to go through the transcript now. I'm putting a very specific question to you. Did you ever receive any orders from anybody else except your superior commander?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, Mr. Milosevic. I always received orders from my immediate superior. At that time it was Colonel Delic, commander of the 549th Motorised Brigade. A few times I received a direct order from the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, who was in Djakovica, and that happened in those cases where a very quick intervention was required and it was not possible to have the regular kind of correspondence. However, that possibility and that right is envisaged in the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Again, very briefly, with regard to these questions, some of which were put by Mr. Bonomy, too, you said that there had not been any activity in Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that what is written is illogical, that the villagers were running or trying to escape up the river, because that would make it impossible for them to run down the river. But let us disregard that, upstream or downstream. Were there any actions or activities that the villagers were fleeing from? Or let me be even more specific: Were the villagers from Bela Crkva fleeing anywhere?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period from the 25th of March onwards, that there were no activities, and I do not have any information to the effect that villagers were fleeing. None of my units observed that. I did not observe that or did I receive any reports about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there anything that they were supposed to flee from?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's as if you asked me whether people were fleeing from Belgrade on that day. Absolutely, if there was no action, what would they be fleeing from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that day and on the following days you did not observe villagers fleeing from Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not observe a single civilian villager, as you call them, leaving Bela Crkva, fleeing from Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice said several times that you received intelligence that there was no activity in Bela Crkva. Is that intelligence or is that information that you got from some of your junior officers?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got it from one of my subordinate officers, the leader of combat security. So this is a junior officer whose battalion commander I was. So in a way all information can be called intelligence, because they portray what the situation in a certain territory is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The -- is that the commander of your combat security that went ahead of you through Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. Ahead of my unit in Bela Crkva, went through Bela Crkva, especially the positions east of the village of Bela Crkva towards the village of Celine, and then he returned with his immediate security, with a few soldiers and one vehicle to the village of Zrze, and he reported to me by the silos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He reported that everything was peaceful and then you went through Bela Crkva how?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marching, on combat vehicles. There was no need for the unit to be deployed for combat or do we ever do that unless there is information that action against the unit is expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Were you the only unit that was in the area during those days or was there another unit of the army of Yugoslavia there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the outskirts of Bela Crkva, that is to say the asphalt road, which I can show - let me just find the map - from Zrze towards Hoca. Sorry, towards Orahovac. Two more groups passed along that road, but they just passed. They did not enter the village itself. As for the village of Bela Crkva, on that morning only my unit passed, as far as the military is concerned, and it was only part of my unit because another part did not even enter Bela Crkva. And part of that 4th Company of the 23rd Detachment of the special units of the police. If necessary, I can show that on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in contact with that company of the special units of the police that was in the same area?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them directly moving through the village of Bela Crkva, also in a column, but they left their motor vehicles, part of their vehicles that was moving in that direction. They left in the area of the silos because there's a big parking lot there. There's enough parking space there, so it's for practical reasons. And then these vehicles were moving along as the combat disposition was moving. So I personally saw them moving, marching through the village in a column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did that unit have any activities in Bela Crkva then?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it certainly did not have any activities if you are referring to combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Any kind of activities that could disturb the civilian population or whatever.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not have any such activity. They didn't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Nice quoted something to you from a book where an officer in a green uniform with three stars was described. Would that have to be a captain of the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of these three stars, I said it could be a captain, a colonel, or a colonel general. But on the basis of the description, I said that in the army there aren't any persons with visible disabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What was the command -- was there any captain commanding any one of your units? You were the only unit that went through Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any captains. There was one captain first class. However, with part of the unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please. Was there an officer with three stars, an officer of yours in that area through Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember. I had two lieutenants, one staff sergeant -- or, rather, two staff sergeants. As far as I can remember, I did not have a single captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You did not have a single captain in your unit in that activity. When I said that, I'm not saying in your unit generally speaking but at that time there, did you have any captain in that activity?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that activity is concerned, I cannot remember who the leader of my anti-aircraft gun platoon was, but a captain could not have commanded a platoon. It would have to have been a non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Was there another military unit that went through Bela Crkva at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through Bela Crkva? Not a single other military unit went through Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, does the rank of captain exist in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it does, but please don't take my word for it. I don't know their ranks. I think it exists, but I don't know what kind of insignia they have. May I say something else? As far as these stars are concerned, we did not wear stars on our uniforms. Stars are usually worn on the official uniforms worn but not on wartime uniforms. So I really express my doubts about that person who says he saw this could have seen stars, you see, because on war uniforms you wear completely different insignia. There's a badge and then a captain has three brass lines, perhaps four or five centimetres long and a few millimetres wide, and they are put together. But you cannot see that either, because in combat you wear combat jackets, and the combat jacket covers the insignia. But not a single officer or NCO had insignia on their war uniforms. That is the way it is in the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about a combat camouflage uniform with the basic colour of green?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: M83, M89, and so on. Those are the models. Green is the base colour, but there are other camouflage colours, like black, brown, dark green, light green, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Colonel. What can be derived from all of this, that there wasn't even a theoretical possibility for a captain of the army of Yugoslavia to have three stars on his shoulder?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completely exclude that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And thank you for reminding me of these war uniforms or combat uniforms, that there are no stars there but only these badges.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, if I can respond to the question that you put: The police does have the rank of captain, but a police captain does not wear a green uniform but a blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to note that Mr. Vukovic did not answer that way when I asked the same question. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic. The witness said that a captain in the VJ would wear three stars on his shoulders, and I did not qualify further. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, lest there be any misunderstanding, all captains have three stars on their shoulders, but that is on their regular uniforms, not on their camouflage combat uniforms. On combat uniforms, there aren't any stars, there are three stripes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have heard that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like now to dwell for a moment on the war diary of yours and the addition, the supplement that Mr. Nice spent time on. Would you turn to page -- I don't see the page number here, but -- there's a hole covering the page number on my copy, but it is the addition to the war diary for the 25th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. The 26th comes after. And that's what Mr. Nice quoted, and it says here -- what does it say here? As it was dealt with in the cross-examination many times here, tell us what it says. Blocked -- what does it say?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A march along the Zub-Djakovica axis took place."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just where it says "Blocked and cleaned the villages of Bela Crkva ..."

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... the villages of Bela Crkva, Celine, Nogavac, and part of Velika Krusa. There were no casualties, no losses."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you gave us an explanation which it was my impression was not sufficient, so I'm going to ask you to give us a broader explanation now. You explained to us that at the time at the command post there was your deputy there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was precisely it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that by using a radio you sent a brief message to him. How long was the message, several seconds' duration?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ten to 15 seconds, not longer than that, otherwise our positions would be found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Anyway, you told us that you had told him where your location was at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of the day I informed him at what line I was, and I used a coded map that he had, too, so he was able to pinpoint the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you just provided him information about where you were, where your location was.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that we had suffered no losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Your position, you used the radio to tell him, "I am at such-and-such a position. I have no losses." Is that all you told him?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was all, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you explained to us that when it says blocked and cleaned -- blocked and -- the following villages were blocked and cleaned, you said that was based on an order that he said.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the brigade commander's order that he had with him too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's take a look at the order issued by the brigade commander. You said, "I've reached such-and-such a position. I have no losses," and then he introduced this record that the villages of Bela Crkva, et cetera, were blocked and cleaned. Now, what does it say in the actual order of the brigade commander that he had with him? You both had the same copy. What does it say on page 2? And that's tab 3.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just take a moment to find the document and open my binder? The only copy of the order, to be quite precise, was the copy that he had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that was the basic command post. Now, tell me what point you wish me to address and read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Read out what it says under point 4, "I have decided ..." Where it says 4, decision, "I have decided ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Mr. Kwon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Colonel, pay attention now and read out that paragraph. It's point 4, it's not a long one, where it says, "I have decided ..." It is number 4, decision by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I have decided: In cooperation with the 37th Detachment of the PJP Nis, the 5th Company of Prizren, the 4th Company of PJP Djakovica, to execute a deblockade of the communication line Suva Reka-Orahovac and to block and destroy the STS, the Siptar forces in the broader region of the village of Retimlje and to establish control over the territory in that area by grouping the main forces along the axes of Studencani-Samodreza and Opterusa-Retimlje, and the auxiliary forces along the following axes: Bela Crkva-Celine-Nogavac, Velika Hoca-Mala Hoca, and then the next axis, the Wine Cellar-Pirane-Zojic, et cetera, Medvedce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, was one of the axes here, the main axis is not one we're interested in at the moment but it says auxiliary forces along the axis, the following axis, and then what does it say?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Bela Crkva --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We're not interested in the first axis, we're interested in --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bela Crkva-Celine-Nogavac, that is the axis along which my unit went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after Nogavac there was Velika Hoca?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Velika Hoca is the next axis. It is to the north of the previous axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, if you told him that you were at such-and-such a position on the -- evening of the 25th, what position were you at?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the evening of the 24th, Mr. Milosevic, I had reached -- that is to say we had gained control of the village of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find the map and I'll tell you, just a moment, please, for that particular day. This is a map that is marked Retimlje, and I have it under number 14, tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sure the Court will have this in mind, this is, of course, not a contemporaneous document so he's simply relying on a map that's been produced by or for the commission from other materials. So I don't see, frankly, how it can assist him. Indeed, I might as well make the point now: None of this commission documentation is probably such as meets the standard requirements of documents that can refresh memory, and I simply don't understand how he can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's an objection then, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, the problem with the commission documents is that they've been coming in over time and we've only been getting to hear, over time, a little bit more about the way the commission worked and what it was doing, but it is perfectly apparent that witnesses are coming here being given all sorts of material. This witness was given statements plans, maps of one kind or another, not prepared by him as far as we know. We don't have the draftsmen, we don't know what raw material they were relying on, we've suddenly discovered that there are indeed contemporaneous working maps that have not been produced to us, and apparently not to these people, and how this documentation can properly be relied on to refresh memory I simply don't know. Of course the standards and tests here are different from those in the standard system but one could probably confidently assert that if somebody sought to rely on a document like this to refresh memory under the traditional rules of memory refreshing documents, he would not be allowed to do so unless he could trace it as a document he himself built on contemporaneous records of his own or the reliability of which he could justify. So I do object, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, please, we're not going to rely on the map.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can rely on this map here, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is a contemporaneous map?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a contemporaneous map. I didn't wish to refresh my memory, what I wanted to do was to illustrate what I was saying, and I'll indicate that and demonstrate it on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in hearing your answer to the following question: What position were you at from which you told your deputy that you were on the evening of the 25th? Where did you tell him you were on the 25th in the evening?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take a look at this here, it is to the east -- just a moment. Let me find the village of Celine - there it is - and it is this position here. It says Brinja, and then there's a trig point, trig 337, towards the Blini [phoen] feature. So we -- and you have a point to the east of -- or south-east of Blini 500 to -- metres to 1 kilometre, feature 450. Now why do I need map? Well, I cannot remember all the trig points, can I? I can't be expected to remember them, but if need be I can take everybody in the courtroom here today and take them on location and show them where that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's dwell on this for a moment. You -- you call it a feature. It was in fact a hill, as far as I can see. You give it the military term. And this trig 450 that you mentioned. Now, did you come from the direction of the west -- from the west towards the south-east or east? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The general axis, the general direction was west-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we were to draw -- or, rather, if you say I reached that point Brinja trig 450, it's several hundred metres away one from another, all along this north/south line, now, if your deputy received information for you to the effect that you were at Brinja and trig 450, along that line there, that axis there, that you had reached that point, can he, on the basis of that, see the passage, the route you had to traverse before that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. And my deputy was fully cognisant of my assignment and task, and he took part in the decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, on this map can we see all the places that he introduced into the war diary, the entries he made in the war diary? Among the places, the localities, which if we place our hand on Brinja and trig 450, can we see that you traversed the following route: Bela Crkva, Celine, Nogavac, and part of Velika Krusa? Is that visible? Can that be seen?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what can be seen, and that's the only thing that he could have known on the basis of his map. That's what he could have concluded on the basis of the order by the brigade commander and the map provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when he heard you telling him that you were at a feature 450 and Brinja, he was able to conclude that you had passed through --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no. This is leading and tendentious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe he should call the deputy if he wants to deal with it, rather than dealing with it in this way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... conclude that. That's leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Mr. Robinson, a moment ago the witness said that the order by the brigade commander was at the command post of the brigade with his deputy, the deputy had it. The witness said that -- he on the evening of the 25th, he told him what location he was at. Those are material facts. I can't move Brinja nor can I move feature 450. We can see that that axis, that direction of Brinja and trig 450 is east of Bela Crkva and Celine and the whole of that order -- area which, according to the order, they should have passed by. Since that, too, is an officer of the army of Yugoslavia who knows the order full well, he knows what his unit is doing, and if he's told, "We're here," that means that he knows the route that they would have had to traverse to reach that point and they are the places that are contained in the additions to the war diary. So it's not a leading question at all, it's just a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We already have the evidence from the witness as to what could have been seen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not what could have been seen, Mr. Robinson. It's quite clear here that if it says in the order that you're supposed to pass by features A, B, C, and D and you report that you are at a feature E, then the person introducing the points knows that you will have to have passed A, B, C, D in order to reach E. That's elementary. Because he has the order and on his working map he has the orders, contemporaneous ones, and recorded what the unit is doing. And he has that same map at the command post of the brigade, at the headquarters and staff there. So I assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Elementary or not, it's for him to tell us, not you. A leading question is a question in which you give the witness the answer, and you're not supposed to do that when you're re-examining, and that's precisely what you were doing and precisely what was objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's also this point, I think, that the whole line of re-examination is premised on a mere possibility raised by this witness as to how the entry for cleansing Bela Crkva arose. There's absolutely no evidence that it was created by reference to the original order. None whatsoever. It's mere supposition. So we're now building on supposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Move on. And no leading questions.
